claims.text: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 forms multiple primary non-eutectic crystalline phases under cooling rates of 52–3018 K/s.
Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 undergoes a complex, multistep crystallization sequence.
Melt-spinning can be used to process the alloy at cooling rates above 10^6 K/s.
Cooling Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 above 10^6 K/s will suppress primary crystallization and increase amorphous retention.
Changing cooling rate can alter phase composition in high-entropy alloys.
Extreme cooling minimizes atomic mobility and diffusion in Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
Reduced atomic mobility prevents sufficient nucleation and growth of crystalline phases.
Ultra-rapid quenching locks the alloy into a metastable amorphous state by reducing the time available for atomic reorganization.
The rapidly quenched alloy will be predominantly amorphous.
The rapidly quenched alloy will exhibit improved thermal stability during controlled low-temperature reheating.
XRD and DSC will show significantly reduced primary-crystallization signals after quenching above 10^6 K/s.
The rapidly quenched samples will show a delayed or suppressed exothermic crystallization onset relative to samples cooled at 52 K/s or 3018 K/s.
The intervention is effective only above an approximately 10^6 K/s cooling-rate threshold.
Keeping reheating below approximately 0.9 Tg will prevent reactivation of crystallization.
Deviation from the specified cooling or reheating boundaries may promote crystallization or introduce internal stresses.
Ultra-rapid quenching may introduce internal stresses or microstructural inhomogeneities that affect mechanical properties.

contradictions.description: The reheating protocol is restricted to temperatures below the crystallization onset, yet the hypothesis proposes measuring whether that onset is delayed or suppressed and lists determination of onset temperature as a measurement. An onset cannot be determined decisively without heating through the relevant transition range.

The hypothesis treats reduced DSC crystallization signals as evidence of amorphous retention and similar or stronger exotherms as evidence against it, but DSC exotherm magnitude is not explicitly separated from onset temperature or residual amorphous fraction. Thus the stated DSC interpretation is internally ambiguous and may not track the claimed crystalline phase volume.
